extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in the philosophy of humour, book reviews, and cultural/political criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A critical book-review-style analysis of philosophical theories of humour (superiority, relief, incongruity) and their social/political implications, offering evaluative claims about what humour is and what it does. The page discusses criteria for what counts as a good/important joke and theoretical strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises 'from feelings of superiority over other people' — exemplified by Plato, Aristotle, Quintillian and Hobbes: 'sudaine Glory arising from some suddaine Conception of some Eminency in our selves, by Comparison with the Infirmityes of others...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this historical framework to evaluate jokes that depend on mockery, denigration, or expressions of superiority. The reviewer notes its core assumption (we do not consider ourselves all equal) and implies political/ethical objectionability from a leftist egalitarian standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a 'release of pent-up nervous energy' (Herbert Spencer; Freud's Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious) where discharged energy provides pleasure by economizing energy ordinarily used to repress psychic activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this account skeptically: the reviewer calls it the weakest of the three ('allegedly' in the source) and says it is 'never explained with any sufficiency' — i.e., avoid relying solely on relief explanations when evaluating humour's functions or mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is produced by the experience of a felt incongruity between what we know or expect to be the case, and what actually takes place (traced to Hutcheson and elaborated by Kant, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard): 'Humor in its first analysis is a perception of the incongruous'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incongruity as a primary analytic tool for identifying joke structure: what expectations are set and how they are subverted. The reviewer treats this as more substantial than relief theory but notes its metaphysical assumptions (underlying order to be disrupted) may be ideologically fraught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenology of the joke / tacit social contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Joking 'is a specific and meaningful practice that the audience and the joke-teller recognize as such' and there is 'a tacit social contract... some agreement about the social world ... as the implicit background to the joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes by whether both teller and audience share the implicit background/world that makes the joke intelligible; consider the rules of the 'game' — jokes succeed only when participants 'both understand and follow the rules.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared-culture requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Joking requires a shared culture; 'in listening to a joke, I am presupposing a social world that is shared' — making humour 'ostensive untranslatability' and reliant on cultural insider-knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke's background assumptions are accessible to its intended audience. The reviewer argues multiculturalism threatens humour's functioning because common background knowledge is eroded; for production, target a defined cultural field or make background explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/comic joke as liberation/transformative
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real comedian' is 'a daring man' whose 'true joke... has to do more than release tension, it has to liberate the will and the desire, it has to change the situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge higher the jokes or comedy that do more than provide relief — those that voice truths listeners avoid, push boundaries, and suggest or effect social change. Distinguish between mere tension-release gags and comedy that 'says the unsayable' and has emancipatory ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative/social-cohesion function of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour often 'serves to reinforce social consensus' and functions as 'cultural insider-knowledge' that 'endows native speakers with a palpable sense of their cultural distinctiveness or even superiority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humour, consider its role in maintaining norms, excluding outsiders, and promoting group solidarity; recognize that many successful jokes work by reinforcing, not undermining, existing social structures (sexist or denigrating humour included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter's two-fold (restorative + transformative) claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour both (i) 'returns us to a common, familiar world of shared practices' and (ii) 'indicate[s] how those practices might be transformed or perfected, how things might be otherwise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this dual lens to evaluate comedic work: does it merely reconfirm shared meanings or does it also point toward different possibilities? The reviewer highlights tension between these functions and questions whether humour can coherently require a shared background while aiming to dissolve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism: exploitation of body/being gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour 'functions by exploiting the gap between being a body and having a body, between... the physical and metaphysical aspects of being human' — comic effect arises when the physical returns the metaphysical to ridiculousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze comedic material for moments where high-minded or metaphysical pretensions are punctured by bodily/physical reality; such collapses often produce the comic effect and connect to tragicomic reflections on human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — incoherent normative claims about humour's purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the view that humour both requires a shared social structure and should 'dispose of' that same structure — 'Can it really be the purpose of humor to create a world in which nothing is funny?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of theoretical claims that prescribe an ideal social function for humour which contradicts empirical descriptions of how humour operates. Avoid arguing both that humour depends on X and that its purpose is to eliminate X without resolving the contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all humour is transformative — many jokes are reactionary
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is important to recognize that not all humour is of this type, and most of the best jokes are fairly reactionary or, at best, simply serve to reinforce social consensus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, don't universalize from politically radical or emancipatory examples; classify humour types and note that 'best' or 'successful' jokes often function conservatively. Production-wise, expect many audiences to prefer consensus-reinforcing jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as an insulation/identity marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a common sense of humour is 'like sharing a secret code' and 'We wear our cultural distinctiveness like an insulation layer against the surrounding alien environment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying or creating humour, account for its role in identity formation and boundary maintenance. Jokes can be tools of cultural cohesion but also of exclusion; assess social costs when humour demarcates in-groups and out-groups.
